newsitem.title: CANADA: B.C. forest industry losses expected to worsen.
newsitem.headline: B.C. forest industry losses expected to worsen.

text.p: British Columbia's forest companies were poised to slide further into the red in 1997 and the industry urgently needed to restructure and undergo a regulatory overhaul, analysts and officials said on Tuesday.

The earnings outlook for 1997 "is not a pretty picture," said Price Waterhouse forest expert Mike MacCallum. He forecast British Columbia firms would lose about C$450 million this year after an estimated C$250 million loss last year.
Lumber operations would generate losses this year after profits in 1996. Pulp would improve but remain unprofitable, MacCallum predicted.

Roger Wright, managing director of the Hawkins Wright Ltd industry consultancy, said the pulp industry worldwide faced continued price volatility and oversupply. Demand appeared likely to grow less than two percent a year for the next four years, he said.
The industry was also highly fragmented, making uniform pricing structures difficult to implement, he said.

That fragmentation made British Columbia companies ripe for mergers and acquisitions. "I think there is a need for consolidation in British Columbia," said John Chrysikopoulos, director of the paper and forest products at Salomon Brothers.
He predicted that within the next five years up to two-thirds of British Columbia's pulp producers could disappear or be swallowed by competitors.

The case for mergers and acquisitions in part stems from the industry's poor performance. The Canadian paper industry had not generated any profits over the past 10 years and capacity could often be bought for less than the cost of building plants, Chrysikopoulos said.
Rationalization would help companies reduce costs, lower the size of their investments and offer access to wood fiber, he said.
But other officials questioned the potential enthusiasm for forest companies to make acquisitions in British Columbia because of widespread complaints about government-imposed costs and regulation.
The burden "almost drives you to start looking elsewhere," said MacMillan Bloedel Ltd Chief Financial Officer Glenn Ferguson.

Increased regulation had raised logging costs by about 70 percent or C$2.5 billion since 1992, Price Waterhouse's MacCallum said. He predicted the province's 1997 timber harvest would fall 4.4 percent to 75 million cubic meters.
MacMillan Bloedel, Canada's biggest forest products company, had seen its logging costs rise 54 percent over the past three years, Ferguson said.
Chrysikopoulos said the business climate in British Columbia put the province "at the bottom of the attractiveness list" for stock investors.
The British Columbia regulatory framework "is a model for failure," Ferguson said, calling for major changes to the province's stumpage system and forest practices code.
The province and industry are discussing potential changes as part of the government's efforts to boost employment in the sector.

But Doug McArthur, deputy to the provincial premier, told the conference that the government was seeking "adaptive change, adaptive improvement within the general overall policy environment" rather than radical overhaul.
